title: A 19-Year-Old Indian Student Died Under a Car in a Perth Parking Lot. She Is Not the Only One.
excerpt: Komalpreet Kaur's death in Australia adds to a grim toll of Indian students killed abroad. The families who sent them are left with grief, distance and unanswered questions.
body:
Komalpreet Kaur, a 19-year-old Indian student, died after being struck by a car and trapped underneath the vehicle in Perth's southern suburbs last Saturday night. The accident — at the Bentley Plaza car park on Albany Highway, near Curtin University — has renewed anguished conversations in the Indian diaspora about the safety of young students sent abroad to build futures their families cannot always witness.

## What Happened

Western Australia Police said the incident occurred at approximately 11:30 PM on Saturday. Kaur was in the car park area when she was hit by a vehicle and became trapped beneath it. Emergency services responded but were unable to save her. Police are investigating the circumstances and have appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Few other details have been released. Kaur's family in India has been notified, and the Indian Consulate in Perth is understood to be assisting with the repatriation process. Friends and community members in Perth's Indian student community have expressed shock, with several social media tributes describing her as warm, ambitious and recently arrived in Australia.

## A Pattern That Refuses to Break

Kaur's death is not an isolated tragedy. It arrives amid a grim and growing catalogue of Indian student deaths abroad — road accidents, assaults, workplace incidents and, in some cases, circumstances that remain unexplained months later. In the United States alone, at least five Indian-origin students have died in separate incidents this year. In Canada, a student was killed during a carjacking. In the UK, a PhD researcher died in a road collision.

Australia, which hosts over 100,000 Indian students — making them the country's largest international student cohort — has faced particular scrutiny. Last year, an Indian student in Melbourne was attacked with iron rods in what police described as a targeted assault. Reports of racial harassment, exploitative employment conditions and inadequate campus safety have periodically surfaced, prompting the Indian government to take up the issue diplomatically.

## The Families Left Behind

For tens of thousands of Indian families, sending a child abroad for education represents the single largest financial and emotional investment of their lives. Parents in Punjab, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala take out loans, sell assets and borrow from extended family to fund tuition fees that can exceed ₹20-30 lakh per year.

The implicit bargain is that a foreign degree will open doors: a better job, a permanent residency pathway, a transformed family trajectory. When that bargain ends in a phone call from a foreign hospital or police station, the devastation is total.

What makes these losses especially cruel is the information gap. Many families have limited ability to navigate foreign legal systems, coordinate with local authorities or even understand the circumstances of what happened. Language barriers, time-zone differences and the sheer distance compound the grief with helplessness.

## What the Indian Government Is Doing — and Not Doing

India's Ministry of External Affairs has expanded its network of consular services in major student destinations, and a 24/7 helpline (1800-11-3090) exists for Indians abroad. The government has also raised safety concerns in bilateral discussions with Australia, Canada and the UK.

But diaspora advocacy groups argue that the response remains reactive rather than preventive. There is no centralised tracking system for Indian student deaths abroad, no mandatory pre-departure safety briefing that covers real-world risks beyond visa paperwork, and no formal mechanism to hold foreign institutions accountable for campus and surrounding-area safety.

Some community leaders have called for India to negotiate bilateral agreements that would require host countries to provide transparent data on crimes against Indian nationals, similar to frameworks that exist for other large diaspora populations.

## What NRIs and Student Families Should Know

For students already abroad or preparing to leave, practical steps matter more than policy debates. Registering with the nearest Indian consulate or high commission is essential — it ensures the government knows you exist and can reach you in an emergency. Understanding local road safety rules, particularly in countries where driving is on the opposite side, can be life-saving. Many Indian students arrive in Australia or the UK without fully internalising that traffic flows differently.

Community networks — student associations, gurdwara and temple groups, Indian cultural organisations — remain the most reliable safety net. They provide not just social connection but practical assistance in emergencies.

Komalpreet Kaur was 19, newly arrived, and by all accounts eager to build the kind of life her family had sacrificed for. She deserved better. So do the thousands of Indian students who will board flights this year with the same hopes and the same vulnerabilities.
